reasoning_traces.think: Chapter window 3 (pages 11–15) introduces foundational viability theory through differential inclusions and constraint satisfaction. The core concept revolves around the viability of solutions to x' ∈ F(t, x) under set-valued constraints P(t). The paper establishes that viability depends on tangency conditions—specifically, condition (3.10) in Theorem 3.3—which ensures that trajectories remain within P(t) for all t ∈ [t₀, T]. These conditions are shown to be sufficient but not necessarily minimal, prompting exploration of alternative necessary and sufficient criteria. The derivation proceeds via Nagumo’s approach, extending earlier work in static constraints to time-varying ones. Notably, the paper distinguishes between classical and generalized tangency conditions, emphasizing their role in defining viable sets. The extension to tubes (time-dependent constraints) necessitates left absolute continuity of P(t), leading to refined definitions of approximate solutions. In contrast to prior literature, this chapter avoids reliance on reachable sets—a computationally burdensome construct—by employing Aumann integrals instead. The final section transitions into Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman theory, linking viability with optimal control through value functions. This framework enables formalizing decision-making under uncertainty, particularly relevant for GSE’s state-transition modeling and GSI’s probabilistic inference engines. The core argument begins with Theorem 4.4 establishing necessary conditions for value functions, followed by Theorem 4.5 ensuring absolute continuity under domain closure and continuity assumptions. Proposition 4.6 introduces the set-valued map F derived from the conjugate Hamiltonian, verifying key properties including (3.12) and (4.5). The proof constructs P_i(t) using separation theorems and continuity of H(t, x, -), leading to measurable selection results via Theorem 8.2.41. The differential inclusion xl(t) ∈ F(t, x(t)) provides a dynamical interpretation of the value function's evolution. The equivalence between viscosity solutions and value functions is established through Theorem 4.7, which connects the differential inclusion to the Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman framework. Corollary 4.9 extends these results to locally Lipschitz functions, offering a more general setting for practical applications. This chapter thus unifies classical optimal control theory with modern viscosity solution techniques, providing a robust foundation for both theoretical analysis and computational implementation in GSI and GSE systems.
